title: Star Tiger
subtitle: Star Tiger · North Atlantic, 1948
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, the open North Atlantic at night in the late 1940s, moonlit towering cloud and dark sea, cold blue-grey and silver tones with a faint amber glow, melancholy and uncanny, vertical 9:16 full-bleed composition with one centred subject in the middle third, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: The Atlantic, January nineteen forty-eight. A British airliner, the Star Tiger, was flying through the night to Bermuda. It never arrived.
beats.img: Vertical full-bleed scene: a single 1940s four-engine propeller airliner with a long silver fuselage and twin tail fins, an Avro Tudor, centred in the middle third of the frame and clearly lit by bright moonlight, flying level through a break in towering night clouds high above a dark ocean, propellers blurred, cabin windows faintly glowing amber, the whole aircraft sharply legible against the cloud, no markings, no lettering.

beats.vo: Just after three in the morning, she asked Bermuda for a radio bearing. Nothing more was heard.
beats.img: Vertical full-bleed scene: inside the dim cockpit radio station of a 1940s airliner at night, an old valve radio receiver with a softly glowing amber dial centred in frame, a brass Morse key and a pair of headphones resting on the small desk, a dark window showing only night cloud, no people, no legible text.

beats.vo: Thirty-one people were aboard. The search found no wreckage. No one aboard was ever seen again.
beats.img: Vertical full-bleed scene: a lone 1940s four-engine search aircraft centred in frame, flying low over a vast empty grey Atlantic at first light, long swells and whitecaps below with nothing on the water, cold pale dawn breaking through overcast, no people.

beats.vo: The official inquiry wrote that no more baffling problem had ever been presented for investigation.
beats.img: Vertical full-bleed scene: a thick closed 1940s government report bound with faded ribbon, centred on a dark wooden table in an empty wood-panelled hearing room, a single brass desk lamp casting warm light across it, rows of empty chairs fading into shadow, no people, no legible text.

beats.vo: Theories include fuel running out, and sabotage. The wreck has never been found.
beats.img: Vertical full-bleed scene: the calm empty Atlantic at night seen from low above the water, a single shaft of moonlight through a gap in heavy cloud falling on the dark sea in the centre of the frame, nothing on the surface, cold silver and blue-grey, silent and unresolved.

facts.claim: Star Tiger was a British South American Airways (BSAA) Avro Tudor IV, G-AHNP, lost early on 30 January 1948 on an overnight flight from Santa Maria in the Azores to Bermuda; it never arrived
Last contact at about 03:15-03:17 when radio officer requested/acknowledged a radio bearing from Bermuda; nothing more was heard
Search (26 aircraft, 882 hours, five days per Wikipedia) found no wreckage and no trace of the aircraft or anyone aboard

Official inquiry (Lord Macmillan, Ministry of Civil Aviation, reported Aug 1948): 'In closing this report it may truly be said that no more baffling problem has ever been presented for investigation' ... 'the fate of Star Tiger must remain an unsolved mystery'
Theories include fuel exhaustion (e.g. 2009 Tom Mangold BBC programme) and sabotage (claimed by Don Bennett / Roy Dobson; rejected by investigators) — theories only
Still unsolved as of 2026: no wreck ever found; no 2020-2026 wreck find reported; 2026 coverage still treats it as unsolved
